newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine and Russia face row over alleged letter.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine and Russia face row over alleged letter.

text.p: A diplomatic row was brewing between Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday over the publication of a document purporting to be a letter from a Russian official proposing plans to oust Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma.
The publication threatened to aggravate relations already difficult because of the two countries' failure to agree how to divide the former Soviet Black Sea Fleet.

The Ukrainian newspaper Vseukrainskiye Vedomosti published the text and a photograph of what it said was a letter from Russian deputy foreign minister Sergei Krylov to President Boris Yeltsin's chief foreign policy adviser, Dmitry Ryurikov.

The letter said Kuchma's policy was "anti-Russian and destructive" and suggested summoning leaders of Russia's two houses of parliament to discuss coordinating efforts to discredit him and prompt Ukraine's parliament to impeach him.
Krylov denied he had written the letter. He told Interfax news agency: "It is a falsification. Such a document does not and could not exist because Ukraine is a friendly state for us."
"The president of Ukraine sincerely wants to solve the difficult problems in Russian-Ukrainian relations," he said.
Authorities in both Ukraine and Russia, who have failed to sign a friendship treaty since the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, reacted strongly.

"I would like to say categorically that this publication is openly provocative. It is in essence a falsification, Goebbels-like propaganda," the Russian foreign ministry said in a statement, referring to Nazi Germany's propaganda minister.

"As this publication appeared in the Ukrainian press, we request that the responsible bodies in Ukraine investigate the circumstances behind its appearance and tell the general public who is behind this provocation."
Ukrainian deputy foreign minister Volodymyr Handogiy told a news briefing in Kiev that Ukraine's ambassador to Moscow had been asked to request an official explanation from Russia.
"We are very concerned about this. If the contents of the article are true, such a position does not correspond to the norms of civilised manners of diplomacy," he said.
"We are concerned at these influential Russian figures' way of thinking."
The editor of Vseukrainskiye Vedemosti, which has good links with Ukraine's president and government, vouched for the authenticity of the letter.
Kuchma is due at the end of this month to attend a summit in Moscow of the leaders of the 12 former Soviet republics which make up the loose Commonwealth of Independent States.
He is expected to hold separate talks with Boris Yeltsin if the Russian president, who has pneumonia, is well enough.

Yeltsin had promised to make Ukraine his first port of call after recovering from the heart problems which dogged him last year. But he wants the Black Sea Fleet row solved first, so that the visit can be crowned by the signing of a friendship treaty.
No dates for the visit have been set.
